entries.title: Error Categories
entries.picture: Four lamps on the bridge panel, and each one starts a different drill.
entries.analogy: Squall passing — hold and try again. Wrong coordinates typed — fix the numbers, do not repeat them. Harbour refusing entry on the rules — no amount of asking changes it. No key for the door — go and find someone who has one.
entries.snapback: Transient → retry. Validation → fix the input. Business → explain the outcome, never retry. Permission → escalate or change credentials.

entries.title: Error-handling Anti-patterns
entries.picture: A crew member who radios 'all fine' with the engine room already flooding.
entries.analogy: Two ways to sink a ship. Say nothing and hope somebody notices the list. Or abandon the whole vessel because one pump failed. Both are on the panel; neither is on the training course.
entries.snapback: Never catch an error and return success. Never terminate the whole workflow for one subagent failure. Never hand back a bare 'failed' with nothing attached.

entries.title: A Structured Subagent Error
entries.picture: A full radio call: what broke, what was tried, what still works, what to do next.
entries.analogy: 'Problem down here' gets you nothing. 'Engine room flooding, valve three shut, pumps holding at forty per cent, recommend rerouting to the aft pumps' gets you a decision from the bridge in about four seconds.
entries.snapback: Return failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and the alternatives worth trying. That is what lets the coordinator choose retry, reroute, continue or escalate.

entries.title: Coverage Annotations in the Final Synthesis
entries.picture: A chart with two areas surveyed properly and one marked 'sounding not taken'.
entries.analogy: You do not throw the chart away because one bay was too rough to sound. You draw what you surveyed, and you write across the bay that nobody has been in there — so the next skipper knows exactly how much to trust it.
entries.snapback: Complete the synthesis on what arrived, mark which conclusions are well supported and where the gaps are, and pass the uncertainty upward.

entries.title: Extract Facts into a Separate Block
entries.picture: A passport pouch on a strap, never buried in the pack.
entries.analogy: Everything else can be rolled, squashed and repacked at the hostel. The passport, the booking reference and the allergy card live in the pouch on the outside, where nothing that happens to the rucksack can touch them.
entries.snapback: Pull transactional facts — amounts, dates, IDs, agreed terms — into a case-facts block included in every prompt, outside the summarised history.

entries.title: Trimming Tool Results
entries.picture: Food out of its boxes, boxes in the bin, before the pack is closed.
entries.analogy: Forty fields came back and five of them matter. Carrying the other thirty-five is not free — you pay for the weight on every step of every day that follows, and it makes the useful five harder to find.
entries.snapback: Trim tool output to the relevant fields with a PostToolUse hook, before it enters context. Choose what to keep from what downstream actually uses.

entries.title: Position-aware Input
entries.picture: You remember what is at the top of the pack and what is at the bottom.
entries.analogy: Whatever went in the middle at four in the morning is gone until you unpack the whole thing on a hostel floor. So the head torch goes in the lid, and the map goes in the front pocket.
entries.snapback: Attention is reliable at the beginning and end of long input and degrades in the middle. Put a key-findings summary at the start and add explicit section headings throughout.

entries.title: Scratchpad Files
entries.picture: A trail journal you write in each night and read each morning.
entries.analogy: Six weeks in, you cannot hold every river crossing in your head, and the version in your head has quietly turned into 'rivers are usually fine'. The journal still says which one had the rope.
entries.snapback: Write intermediate findings to a scratchpad file and read it back at each continuation. It survives context limits and stops the drift into vague generalities.

entries.title: Delegating to Subagents to Protect Context
entries.picture: Sending someone ahead to scout, who comes back with one paragraph.
entries.analogy: You do not all walk the eight kilometres to find out whether the bridge is standing. One person goes, sees everything, and comes back with a sentence. The rest of you are still fresh when it matters.
entries.snapback: Run verbose discovery in a subagent so the output never enters the main window. It returns a concise summary and the main session keeps its capacity for the work.

entries.title: Structured State Persistence
entries.picture: Cairns left along the route, and a note at base camp saying who has reached where.
entries.analogy: Someone twists an ankle four hours from the end. Nobody restarts from the trailhead — you read the note at base, see three parties are through the pass and one is not, and you carry on from there.
entries.snapback: Each agent exports structured state — status, findings, coverage, gaps — to a known location, and the coordinator loads a manifest on resume and continues from the checkpoint.

entries.title: The Attribution Loss Problem
entries.picture: An exhibit bag with the label torn off.
entries.analogy: The evidence is genuine. Nobody can say where it came from, who handled it, or when. In a courtroom that makes it worthless, and a list of everywhere you went that day does not fix it.
entries.snapback: Require structured claim-to-source mappings from every subagent and require synthesis to preserve them. A bibliography records what was read, not which source produced this claim.

entries.title: Handling Conflicting Data
entries.picture: Two witness statements entered into the record side by side, both signed.
entries.analogy: Two credible witnesses give different numbers. The clerk does not average them, and does not quietly pick the one from the more impressive address. Both go in the record, attributed, and somebody senior decides.
entries.snapback: Complete the analysis carrying both values with attribution, and annotate the conflict explicitly. Do not resolve it by heuristic and do not block waiting for a ruling.

entries.title: Include Dates for Correct Interpretation
entries.picture: Two statements that contradict each other until you read the dates on them.
entries.analogy: One says ten per cent, the other fifteen. Enormous scandal, until somebody turns the pages over and finds they were taken a year apart. Then it stops being a contradiction and starts being growth.
entries.snapback: Require publication or collection dates in every structured output. Without them, ordinary change over time gets reported as sources disagreeing.

entries.title: Render by Content Type
entries.picture: You do not read a spreadsheet aloud as a story.
entries.analogy: Financials go in the exhibit table where the columns line up. The account of what happened goes in prose. Read the table out as a flowing narrative and everyone in the room loses the numbers.
entries.snapback: Financial and tabular data as tables, news and analysis as prose, technical findings as structured lists, time series in chronological order.

entries.title: Tool Selection Reference
entries.picture: The catalogue drawer next to a full-text search of every page.
entries.analogy: The catalogue finds books by title and shelf mark. It cannot tell you which books mention a name on page ninety. For that you need something that reads inside, and asking the catalogue will get you a confident, wrong, very short answer.
entries.snapback: Glob matches file paths. Grep searches file contents. 'Which files use this function' is a content question, so it is Grep — every time.

entries.title: Incremental Investigation Strategy
entries.picture: Following the citations, rather than reading the whole floor.
entries.analogy: You have one afternoon and eleven thousand books. You find one paper on the subject, read its references, pull those three, read theirs. You do not begin at shelf A and work east.
entries.snapback: Grep to locate entry points, Read the files you found, Grep for their usages, Read those. Reading everything up front to 'get full context' is the named anti-pattern.

entries.title: Fallback: Read + Write Instead of Edit
entries.picture: A correction that needs a sentence appearing exactly once on the page.
entries.analogy: Tell the archivist to change 'the rate is fixed' and they will ask which of the four. Give them a shorter phrase and it gets worse, not better — now it appears eleven times. So you take the page, retype it whole, and put it back.
entries.snapback: Edit needs a unique anchor. When it fails, Read the file, modify the content, Write it back. A shorter anchor is more likely to be non-unique, not less.
